steps.tx: Surgical management of complex chest and abdominal wall defects requires restoring structural stability and providing vascularised soft tissue coverage. Reconstruction of extensive full-thickness chest wall defects exceeding 5 cm or 4 ribs mandates rigid skeletal stabilization to prevent **paradoxical respiration** and ventilatory failure.
steps.say: A large hole in the chest wall cannot be covered with skin alone. Once the defect passes five centimetres or four missing ribs, the chest needs rigid rebuilding first, because a flail segment that sucks inward on inspiration produces paradoxical breathing and the patient cannot ventilate.

nodes.label: Full-thickness chest or abdominal wall defect

steps.tx: Sternal osteomyelitis and post-sternotomy dehiscence are managed by radical debridement followed by flap reconstruction. The **pectoralis major turnover flap** based on internal mammary perforators or rotation flap based on the thoracoacromial axis provides robust muscle coverage for upper and middle sternal defects.
steps.say: When a sternotomy wound breaks down and the bone becomes infected, cut away every scrap of dead tissue and cover the gap with muscle. The pectoralis major is the first choice for the upper and middle sternum, swung over on its internal mammary perforators or rotated on the thoracoacromial vessels.

vis.alt: Surgical needle holder for sternal wound closure
vis.caption: Surgical suturing instruments for complex sternal and fascial reconstructive closure. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: Lower sternal and anterior chest wall defects are reliably covered by the **rectus abdominis flap** based on the superior epigastric artery, or the greater omentum flap based on the gastroepiploic vessels. The omentum conforms intimately to irregular infected mediastinal cavities and accelerates bacterial clearance.
steps.say: Defects low on the sternum sit beyond the reach of pectoralis, so the repair must turn to the rectus abdominis on the superior epigastric artery, or bring up the greater omentum on the gastroepiploic vessels. Omentum is unmatched in a ragged infected mediastinum because it drapes into every crevice and helps clear bacteria.

steps.tx: In complex ventral hernia repair and large midline abdominal defects, **component separation** allows medial advancement of the rectus abdominis complexes. Ramirez anterior component separation divides the external oblique aponeurosis lateral to the semilunar line, releasing 8 to 10 cm of advancement per side.
steps.say: Closing a giant ventral hernia starts with freeing the rectus muscles to slide toward the midline. In the Ramirez anterior release the surgeon divides the external oblique aponeurosis just outside the semilunar line, which buys eight to ten centimetres of medial movement on each side.

nodes.label: Longitudinal incision of external oblique aponeurosis
Dissection between external and internal oblique muscles
Medial advancement of rectus complex to midline

steps.tx: Posterior component separation, known as the **transversus abdominis release** or TAR technique, incises the posterior lamella of the internal oblique aponeurosis and releases the transversus abdominis muscle, creating a vast retro-rectus vascularised space for giant sublay mesh placement without compromising cutaneous perforators.
steps.say: The posterior alternative is the transversus abdominis release. Cutting the back layer of the internal oblique and dividing the transversus opens a huge well vascularised pocket behind the rectus on each side, room enough for a giant sublay mesh, while the skin perforators coming through the front are never touched.

steps.tx: Surgical mesh reinforcement in abdominal reconstruction follows standard planar positioning. The **retro-rectus sublay** position, placed behind the rectus muscle and anterior to the posterior sheath, is associated with the lowest recurrence and infection rates compared to onlay or intraperitoneal underlay positions.
steps.say: Mesh works best sandwiched behind the rectus and in front of the posterior sheath, the retro-rectus sublay plane. Kept away from both skin and bowel, the mesh sees the lowest rates of infection and of hernia coming back, beating onlay and intraperitoneal positions on both counts.

steps.tx: Massive full-thickness abdominal wall defects where primary fascial reapproximation is impossible require vascularised regional or distant flap reconstruction. The **anterolateral thigh flap** or tensor fasciae latae flap incorporating a robust sheet of vascularised fascia lata provides composite structural support and durable cutaneous coverage.
steps.say: When so much abdominal wall is missing that the fascia cannot be pulled together at all, import new wall as a flap. The tensor fasciae latae or the anterolateral thigh flap can be raised with a sheet of tough fascia lata attached, giving a living patch that holds tension like fascia and carries its own skin cover.

vis.alt: Abdominal wall surgical debridement and reconstruction
vis.caption: Fascial plane dissection and reconstructive debridement in abdominal wall repair. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: Loss of domain in giant ventral hernias poses severe risks of postoperative **abdominal compartment syndrome** upon forced reduction. Preoperative preparation using progressive preoperative pneumoperitoneum or ultrasound-guided botulinum toxin A injections into the lateral abdominal wall muscles relaxes lateral tension and increases intra-abdominal capacity.
steps.say: In a giant hernia much of the bowel lives outside the abdomen, and forcing it all back at once can strangle the circulation, which is the abdominal compartment syndrome. Prepare the belly first: weeks of progressive pneumoperitoneum stretch the cavity, or botulinum toxin injections relax the lateral muscles so they lengthen and the contents can slide home safely.

rows: Lengthens lateral obliques, eases midline closure
